name: Devanagari
signature: A horizontal head-line (shirorekha) runs across the top; letters hang beneath it like laundry on a line.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent 'a' (क = ka). A vowel mark (mātrā) replaces that vowel (क + ी → की = kī). The virama ् strips the vowel, and the bare consonant joins the next into a conjunct (न + ् + म → न्म). The horizontal top line (shirorekhā) runs across the whole word.
notes: Used by Hindi, Marathi, and Sanskrit in this curriculum. The initial inventory below covers the greeting/self-introduction vocabulary; it grows toward a complete set. Stroke orders are the common handwriting convention, not a standard.

strokeOrder: curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
letters.strokeOrderNote: verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the body into more strokes

strokeOrderSource.citation: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari अ stroke order.svg’, frames 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023
strokeOrderSource.variation: The four buildup frames show four ordered pen-down runs: frame 1 starts at the upper-left and carries the upper curve into the lower bowl without lifting; frame 2 restarts at the middle junction and sweeps right through the shoulder; frame 3 descends the right stem top-to-bottom; frame 4 draws the shirorekhā left-to-right, for three intervening lifts. Thomas Egenes, Learning the Sanskrit Alphabet, p. 12 (Maharishi International University Press, 1990), documents a six-stroke traditional Sanskrit form instead. This learner path follows the four-run modern form and fits its joins and directions to Noto Sans Devanagari.

strokeOrderSource.citation: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari आ stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023
strokeOrderSource.variation: The five buildup frames show five ordered pen-down runs: frame 1 starts at the upper-left and carries the upper curve into the lower bowl without lifting; frame 2 restarts at the middle junction and sweeps right through the shoulder; frame 3 descends the inner stem top-to-bottom; frame 4 descends the trailing stem top-to-bottom; frame 5 draws the shirorekhā left-to-right, for four intervening lifts. Thomas Egenes, Learning the Sanskrit Alphabet, p. 12 (Maharishi International University Press, 1990), documents the shared base अ itself as a six-stroke traditional Sanskrit form, so the joined modern body is not universal. This learner path follows the five-run modern form and fits its joins and directions to Noto Sans Devanagari.

components: a descending upright joined to an upper bowl
a lower bowl and diagonal tail in the same run
strokeOrder: descend the upright from the headline, turn left around the upper bowl, sweep right through the waist and around the lower bowl, then finish down-right through the tail without lifting
lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
letters.strokeOrderNote: verified modern printed teaching form; everyday handwriting may simplify the curves

strokeOrderSource.citation: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari इ stroke order.svg’, panels 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023
strokeOrderSource.variation: The two-panel diagram marks the body as one continuous pen-down run: panel 1's green start sits at the top of the upright; its arrows descend the upright, turn left around the upper bowl, sweep right through the waist and around the lower bowl, then finish down-right through the tail without lifting. Panel 2 restarts at the headline's left edge and draws the shirorekhā left-to-right, for one intervening lift. This learner path follows that modern printed teaching form and fits its turns and directions to Noto Sans Devanagari. Other handwriting may simplify the curves, so this is a sourced learner path rather than a universal standard.
